task: Write a conference-style English abstract communicating the distinctive contribution for robot-learning readers, and one Results paragraph. Explain the design and what an informative comparison establishes using only the supplied body material. Choose evidence by function, not a summary of every component or table. Do not invent missing facts, gaps, significance or guarantees. Put unresolved reporting questions in working notes, not generic abstract disclaimers.
sources: Third-party body text excluded; see source_receipts.json and extraction script.

drafts.A: Rotating a manipulation scene changes both the observation and the required gripper motion, but the corresponding transformation depends on whether actions specify absolute poses or relative motions. We introduce Equivariant Diffusion Policy, which encodes this relationship in action denoising. We show that the noise prediction function is equivariant under planar rotations when the expert policy is equivariant, and derive rotation representations for both forms of six-degree-of-freedom control. Equivariant observation and action encoders produce features indexed by discrete rotations; a shared temporal U-Net across those rotations and an equivariant decoder preserve the transformation structure. Across 12 simulated manipulation tasks, the voxel-based policy with absolute control reaches 63.9% average peak success with 100 demonstrations per task, compared with 42.0% for RGB-based standard diffusion policy. Physical-robot evaluation provides a comparison using identical voxel inputs and approximately matched parameter counts: the equivariant policy achieves 80-95% success across six tasks, versus 0-60% for the non-equivariant baseline, using 20-60 demonstrations per task. These results support exploiting rotational structure for data-limited manipulation, while gains with image observations are smaller under relative control.
drafts.B: Exploiting planar symmetry in diffusion-based manipulation requires specifying how gripper poses and action noise transform. We introduce Equivariant Diffusion Policy, grounded in a conditional result: when the expert policy is SO(2)-equivariant and noise transforms like actions, the associated noise predictor is also equivariant. Absolute targets rotate with the scene, whereas relative updates require conjugation because the current pose also rotates; linear representations encode both transformations in the denoiser. The implementation uses a finite rotation subgroup: equivariant encoders produce rotation-indexed observation and action features, a shared temporal U-Net processes corresponding orientations, and an equivariant decoder predicts action noise. Across twelve simulation tasks with 100 demonstrations per task and absolute control, the image model attains 53.7% mean peak success versus 42.0% for the non-equivariant diffusion baseline. Relative-control gains are smaller, and image rotations do not exactly match physical scene rotations. On six physical-robot tasks, the voxel model achieves 80-95% success with 20-60 demonstrations, exceeding a similarly sized non-equivariant policy receiving the same voxel inputs. These comparisons support symmetry-constrained denoising as a useful inductive bias for demonstration-limited manipulation.

drafts.A: With absolute pose control and 100 demonstrations per task, the image-based equivariant policy achieves 53.7% average success across 12 simulation tasks, versus 42.0% for DiffPo-C using the same temporal U-Net backbone. This comparison supports the utility of the architectural symmetry constraint without introducing voxel observations. The voxel version reaches 72.6% with 200 demonstrations, exceeding the strongest baseline's 71.4% with 1,000 demonstrations, although that comparison also changes the observation representation. Simulation values are peak success rates over 50 evaluations during training, averaged across three seeds. On hardware, both policies receive the same voxel grid and have approximately equal parameter counts. With 40 demonstrations, letter alignment succeeds in 19/20 trials for EquiDiff and 0/20 for the non-equivariant policy. All six hardware tasks favor EquiDiff. The benefits are less pronounced for image-based relative control, where average improvements over the best baseline are 2.1-3.7 percentage points across the tested budgets.
drafts.B: With 100 demonstrations per task, image-based EquiDiff achieved 53.7% mean peak success across twelve simulation tasks under absolute control, compared with 42.0% for DiffPo-C, which uses the same RGB observations and temporal U-Net backbone. Simulation results report maxima over 50 evaluations during training and are averaged over three seeds. Under relative control, the corresponding averages were 35.4% and 33.3%, showing that the gain depends on the action convention. On hardware, both policies received the same voxel grid and had approximately matched parameter counts: after 40 demonstrations, EquiDiff completed letter alignment in 19 of 20 trials, whereas the non-equivariant baseline completed none. Across all six hardware tasks, EquiDiff achieved 80-95% success. Together, the RGB simulation comparison and matched-voxel hardware comparison support an architectural benefit beyond simply switching to 3D observations, with substantially smaller gains for image-based relative control.

drafts.A: We present Equivariant Diffusion Policy, a behavior-cloning method that couples planar scene rotations to six-degree-of-freedom gripper actions throughout denoising. When the expert policy is SO(2)-equivariant and noise transforms like actions, the associated noise predictor inherits that equivariance. We derive rotation representations for absolute and relative pose control, whose transformations differ by left multiplication versus conjugation. Equivariant encoders and a decoder surround a temporal U-Net shared across discrete rotation-indexed embeddings, imposing this structure without replacing the temporal backbone. Image and voxel observations provide two implementations; voxel rotations align with state rotations, whereas oblique camera images introduce a symmetry mismatch. On 12 MimicGen tasks, the RGB version reaches 53.7% average peak success with 100 demonstrations per task under absolute control, versus 42.0% for a non-equivariant diffusion policy using the same temporal backbone. The voxel version reaches 72.6% with 200 demonstrations, compared with 71.4% for that RGB baseline with 1,000. Physical experiments compare policies using the same voxel input and approximately matched parameter counts: the equivariant policy achieves 80-95% success across six tasks with 20-60 demonstrations. These results support rotation-structured denoising for data-limited manipulation.
drafts.B: We introduce Equivariant Diffusion Policy, which constrains action denoising to respect planar rotations in manipulation. For an SO(2)-equivariant expert, transforming observations and noisy actions together also transforms the target noise, provided noise follows the action representation. This relationship motivates imposing symmetry on the noise predictor itself. We derive rotation representations for absolute and relative SE(3) gripper commands, then connect equivariant observation and action encoders to a decoder through a temporal U-Net with parameters shared across discrete rotations. The construction respects the different transformation rules of absolute and relative control. Across 12 MimicGen tasks, voxel-input absolute control with 200 demonstrations averages 72.6% peak success over training, exceeding the strongest baseline average with 1,000 demonstrations (71.4%); simulation results average training maxima across three seeds. On six physical-robot tasks with 20-60 demonstrations, success ranges from 80% to 95%, compared with 0%-60% for a similarly sized non-equivariant policy using the same voxels. Benefits are larger in low-data simulation settings, while gains diminish at larger data budgets and sensing can violate the assumed symmetry.

drafts.A: With RGB observations and a temporal U-Net backbone shared by EquiDiff (Im) and DiffPo-C, absolute-control success averages 53.7% versus 42.0% at 100 demonstrations per task across 12 MimicGen environments. These values average, over three seeds, the maximum success rate among 50 evaluations during training. The comparison shows that the low-data gain does not require changing to voxel observations. Control mode matters: at the same demonstration budget, RGB relative-control averages are 35.4% and 33.3%. On hardware, both methods instead receive the same voxel grid, and the non-equivariant baseline has approximately matched trainable parameter counts. With 40 demonstrations, letter alignment succeeds in 19/20 trials for EquiDiff versus 0/20 for the baseline. Bagel baking, trained with 58 demonstrations, succeeds in 16/20 versus 2/20 trials; all EquiDiff failures on that task are attributed to robot joint limits. Together, these comparisons support a benefit from the equivariant architecture beyond voxel input alone, while showing that performance depends on control mode and execution constraints.
drafts.B: Matching the visual representation on hardware shows that the gains are not explained solely by voxel input. With 20-60 demonstrations per task, EquiDiff succeeds in 80%-95% of trials across six tasks, versus 0%-60% for a non-equivariant diffusion policy using the same voxel grid and approximately the same parameter count; each policy receives 20 trials per task. On letter alignment, the contrast is 19/20 versus 0/20. Simulation provides complementary evidence at limited data: with 100 demonstrations and absolute control, the RGB version averages 53.7% success across 12 tasks, compared with 42.0% for DiffPo-C using the same observation type and temporal U-Net backbone. These simulation values average the maximum success over 50 evaluations during training across three seeds. The absolute-control RGB advantage is smaller with more demonstrations, and relative-control RGB gains over the strongest baseline are modest. Together, the comparisons support symmetry-aware denoising under restricted demonstration budgets without attributing the gains simply to a richer visual input.

drafts.A: Re-Mix curates heterogeneous robot demonstration mixtures by learning sampling weights that can be reused across policy training runs without specifying a downstream task. It optimizes worst-case excess imitation loss relative to a reference policy, focusing on domains where the learned policy falls behind the reference rather than on high absolute losses alone. Gaussian action normalization and discretized action likelihoods address mismatched loss scales, multimodal actions, and outlier-sensitive regression losses; validation-based early stopping guards against reference overfitting. The resulting domain weights are transferred to separate diffusion policies, separating data curation from policy architecture. We evaluate on Bridge V2 and the RT-X mixture using WidowX and Franka robots, with local co-training data (25 demonstrations per adaptation task) assigned a total mixture weight of 5%. For RT-X subsets retaining 25% of the data, Re-Mix achieves 80% mean success across four tasks, versus 38% with size-proportional sampling and 33% with expert weights. The two-task full-data Bridge evaluation shows similar performance under Re-Mix and uniform sampling, but quarter-sized subsets favor Re-Mix. These results support action-based curation for the evaluated heterogeneous and data-restricted training settings.
drafts.B: Robot dataset domains can have high imitation losses because actions differ in scale or are difficult to fit, making raw loss an ambiguous basis for selecting a training mixture. Re-Mix learns reusable domain weights through minimax optimization of excess loss relative to a reference policy, prioritizing domains where the learned policy has not yet matched the reference. Gaussian normalization aligns action scales, action discretization addresses multimodality and outliers, and validation-based early stopping keeps the reference informative rather than allowing near-zero training loss to erase this comparison. Averaged weights then train downstream diffusion policies, separating curation from policy learning without requiring a target task during mixture selection. We evaluate RT-X and Bridge V2 mixtures on physical robots with limited co-training: 25 demonstrations for each of three representative tasks contribute 5% of the training mixture. With 25% of RT-X data retained, Re-Mix reaches 80% reported mean success, compared with 38% for uniform subsetting and 33% for expert-weighted subsetting. Full-data Bridge results are similar under Re-Mix and uniform sampling, whereas the subset comparison favors Re-Mix, showing why full-data weighting and data removal must be evaluated separately.

drafts.A: Mixture choice mattered more after subsetting than in the full-data Bridge comparison. With all Bridge data, Re-Mix and uniform sampling produced similar task success; retaining only 25% of the dataset yielded reported mean success of 90% for Re-Mix, 50% for uniform subsetting, and 22% for Self-Supervised Prototypes, which selects trajectories using CLIP image embeddings. At the same retention fraction on RT-X, Re-Mix reached 80%, versus 38% with uniform and 33% with expert-derived subset weights. These contrasts favor the learned weighting procedure over both size-based sampling and visual-diversity selection under the tested data budget, rather than establishing that reweighting always helps. Final diffusion policies shared 400,000 training steps and co-training data comprising 25 demonstrations for each of three representative tasks at 5% mixture weight; evaluation used ten physical executions per task. The findings therefore concern generalization after limited co-training, not zero-shot transfer to the evaluation setups.
drafts.B: At a fixed 25% RT-X data budget, Re-Mix achieves 80% mean success across four hardware tasks, compared with 38% for size-proportional sampling and 33% for expert-defined weights. Final diffusion policies train for 400,000 gradient steps with local demonstrations at 5% mixture weight; each task receives 10 evaluation trials. The comparison therefore measures curation under matched retained-data and training budgets, with learned weights still used for sampling after subsetting. On Bridge, the four-task subset evaluation yields 90% mean success for Re-Mix, versus 50% for uniform sampling and 22% for image-based Self-Supervised Prototypes. In contrast, the two-task full-data Bridge evaluation reports similar performance for learned and uniform weights. The subset comparisons show that retention strategies change downstream performance even at the same data budget. Ablations also link the weighting procedure to its reference: using a checkpoint 50,000 steps after early stopping reduces performance, and replacing discrete actions with continuous actions worsens the subset results.

drafts.A: Robot dataset curation must distinguish domains that offer useful learning progress from those with high imitation loss simply because they are noisy or difficult. We introduce Re-Mix, which learns domain weights through group distributionally robust optimization on loss relative to a reference policy, rather than raw loss. Gaussian normalization aligns action scales across heterogeneous domains, action discretization avoids reliance on outlier-sensitive continuous losses, and early stopping keeps reference losses from collapsing through memorization. Re-Mix returns reusable weights rather than a final policy: weights learned with discrete action models guide both diffusion-policy training and data retention without target-task information. Evaluation uses WidowX and Franka robots, with a 5% in-domain co-training mixture because pretraining alone fails to transfer to the evaluation setups. On RT-X, learned weights outperform uniform and expert-designed mixtures and retain reported performance after reducing the dataset to 25%. On quarter-sized Bridge V2, mean success is 90%, versus 50% for uniform subsetting and 22% for visual-embedding selection. Full-data Bridge weighting produces little difference, showing that the value of curation depends on the data regime.
drafts.B: Re-Mix curates robot demonstration mixtures without selecting data for a known target task. It learns reusable domain weights through minimax optimization of excess imitation loss relative to a reference policy, so weighting depends on the gap to a reference rather than raw domain difficulty. Applying this objective to heterogeneous robot data requires more than importing robust optimization: action scales differ across controllers, continuous losses are sensitive to outliers and multimodal actions, and reference models can memorize limited demonstrations. Re-Mix applies Gaussian action normalization within embodiments, discretizes actions for weight estimation, and selects checkpoints before domain-level overfitting. The resulting weights are reused to train diffusion policies independently of the discrete curation model. Real-robot experiments on RT-X and Bridge V2 use 25 in-domain demonstrations for each of three tasks at a 5% co-training weight. With 25% of RT-X retained, Re-Mix achieves 80% mean success, compared with 38% for uniform and 33% for human-curated weights. Full Bridge training shows little benefit from reweighting, whereas subsetting exposes substantial differences. The findings support learned mixture weights for selective data reduction, with their benefit depending on dataset composition and training regime.

drafts.A: At the same 25% data-retention budget, Re-Mix yields higher reported mean success than alternative curation strategies: 80% versus 38% with uniform and 33% with human-defined weights on RT-X, and 90% versus 50% with uniform and 22% with vision-based SSP on Bridge. Each subset comparison covers four tasks with ten real-robot trials per task. Final diffusion policies train for 400,000 gradient steps and include 25 in-domain demonstrations for each of three representative tasks at a 5% mixture weight; the evaluation tasks test shifts beyond this co-training data. These comparisons show that the composition of a reduced training set matters, rather than data volume alone. In contrast, full Bridge training shows similar performance under Re-Mix and uniform weighting on its two evaluated tasks. The subset ablations further report worse outcomes with continuous-action weight estimation or an overfit reference checkpoint, supporting the discretization and early-stopping choices without identifying either as the sole source of improvement.
drafts.B: Bridge V2 distinguishes improving a mixture from deciding which data can be removed. Learned scene weights and uniform sampling perform similarly on the full dataset's two evaluation tasks. With only 25% retained, however, Re-Mix averages 90% success across four tasks, compared with 50% for uniform subsetting and 22% for Self-Supervised Prototypes, which selects for diversity in visual embeddings. Each task receives 10 physical trials. The final diffusion policies use the same 400,000-step training budget and a 5% co-training mixture containing 25 in-domain demonstrations for each of three tasks. Thus, the subset comparison favors action-informed curation at matched retained volume, rather than more data or training steps. Retention and training-time domain weights change together, so this tests their combined effect. RT-X similarly retains reported performance under Re-Mix subsetting while expert-weighted subsetting loses performance. Since Bridge subsetting adds two tasks, its full-data and quarter-data averages are not paired measurements of the same task set.
